summary: Recommends terminology for use when MPLS Special-Purpose Labels are specified, and applies the change to the relevant IANA registry. It also clarifies the use of the Entropy Label Indicator when it directly follows the Extension Label. It updates RFC 3032 and RFC 7274.

plainLanguage.summary: Some MPLS labels have special jobs. This cleans up the vocabulary so documents describing them are consistent and clear.

subtitle: Clear names for MPLS special-purpose labels, and a fix to how the Entropy Label Indicator is described.

tldr.problem: RFC 7274 changed the terms for MPLS special-purpose labels but did not define consistent terminology, and its text on the Entropy Label Indicator caused confusion.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9017 defines names for the base, extended and composite special-purpose labels, renames one IANA registry, and replaces two paragraphs of RFC 7274 about labels that follow the Extension Label.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 3032 and RFC 7274, changes no forwarding behavior, and gives later documents a common vocabulary.

today: RFC 9017 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2021 that updates RFC 3032 and RFC 7274. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why the Terms Needed Fixing
sections.content:
RFC 7274 changed some of the terminology for MPLS Special-Purpose Labels (SPLs) but did not define consistent terms. It deprecated calling a range of labels "reserved labels", because "Reserved" in an IANA registry means set aside and not to be used, while that range was available for allocation.

When the first draft was written, the IETF was allocating the very first SPLs from the Extended SPL range. RFC 9017 recommends terminology and abbreviations for talking about and documenting SPLs. It updates RFC 3032 and RFC 7274.
sections.plainLanguage: People were calling the same thing by different names. This document picks one name for each kind of label.

sections.title: The Two Sets of Special-Purpose Labels
sections.content:
Two sets of SPLs exist in MPLS. The range 0-15 is specified in RFC 3032. The range 0-1048575 of extended SPLs is specified in RFC 7274. Within that extended range, values 0-15 are reserved and never to be allocated, 16-239 are available for allocation, 240-255 are for experimental use, and 256-1048575 are not currently available. Changing that would need a Standards Track RFC defining the ranges and registration policy.

The RFC also notes that IANA keeps a separate "Special-Purpose Generalized Label Values" registry for GMPLS. Those labels are 32 bits long, are not MPLS forwarding-plane labels, and this document does not change them.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a small box of special labels numbered 0 to 15 and a much bigger box of extra ones. Most of the big box is still locked.

sections.title: The New Names
sections.content:
The conventions to use when specifying and discussing SPLs are:

  • Collectively, the two unrelated ranges (0-15 and 16-1048575) are Special-Purpose Labels (SPLs).
  • SPLs from 0-15 are Base Special-Purpose Labels (bSPLs).
  • SPLs from 16-1048575 are Extended Special-Purpose Labels (eSPLs). The reserved values 0-15 in the extended registry need no name, since they MUST NOT be used.
  • The Extension Label (XL), value 15, is a bSPL also called the xSPL. An XL together with an eSPL is a Composite Special-Purpose Label (cSPL).

The RFC illustrates this with label stacks where a bSPL is a single stack entry, and a cSPL is an XL entry followed by an eSPL entry.
sections.plainLanguage: Little special labels are base labels, the extra ones are extended labels, and a base label that says "another one follows" plus that next label make a composite.

sections.title: Clarifying the Entropy Label Indicator
sections.content:
Section 3.1 of RFC 7274 had two paragraphs on handling the Entropy Label Indicator (ELI, label 7) that confused readers about whether the ELI can follow an Extension Label directly. RFC 9017 replaces them.

The new text says an implementation MUST NOT place a label with a value in the range 0-15 immediately after an XL. An LSR that processes a packet with an XL at the top of the stack followed by a label in the range 0-15 MUST drop the packet. It also notes that a preexisting implementation looking for an ELI may fail to check whether the previous label is an XL. Such a system can keep processing the entropy information and forward the packet without harm, but the packet will be dropped when the XL reaches the top of the stack at another LSR.
sections.plainLanguage: A rule says the label right after the "another one follows" label must not be a reserved one. Older equipment may not notice, but a later stop will throw the packet away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document describes terminology for specifying SPLs. It does not affect forwarding in the MPLS data plane, nor how Label Switched Paths are established by an MPLS control plane or a centralized controller. It does not aim to describe existing SPL implementations or their potential vulnerabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: Because this is only about names, nothing about how packets move changes.

sections.title: IANA Registry Changes
sections.content:
IANA renamed the registry once called "Special-Purpose MPLS Label Values" to "Base Special-Purpose MPLS Label Values". The name of the extended registry and of the enclosing name space are unchanged.

IANA also changed the description of value 15 from "Extension Label" to "Extension Label (XL)" and added RFC 9017 as a reference, so the entry now cites RFC 7274 and RFC 9017.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list got a new title and one entry got a clearer name.
